latin.431: CAPUT VIII. Responsio ad argumenta quae pro Imputatione peccati Actualis Adami ducuntur ex Vetere Testamento Cap. V. Constituto & illustrato, prout tibi visum est, quaestionis statu, tandem, Vir Clarissime, Capite tui tractatus quinto copias argumentorum tuorum educis in aciem, & explicas. Prodeunt autem omnium prima pauca quaedam e Vetere Testamento deprompta.
latin.432: Primum erumpit ex interdicto arboris scientiae boni & mali, & sic procedit. Si interdictum illud, inquis, & comminatio non tantum primos parentes spectavit, sed etiam totum genus humanum, sequitur transgressionem illius Mandati non tantum primos parentes morti obnoxios fecisse, sed etiam totum genus humanum. Atqui verum prius. Ergo & posterius. Prima pars maioris (quae est de interdicto) extra controversiam est: nam quis inficias ibit Dominum legem dedisse non tantum Adamo, sed etiam posteris omnibus? quis negabit lege illa interdictum omnibus hominibus esum illius fructus? Consequentia vero manifesta est ex eventu: Nam violato interdicto, & Adam & omnes posteri morti obnoxii facti sunt. Principio huius tui argumenti conclusionem concedo: est enim tam meae quam tuae sententiae amica. Credo tecum firmiter, transgressionem Adami non tantum primos parentes morti obnoxios fecisse, sed etiam totum genus humanum. Sed quaestio est inter nos duntaxat de modo, quo transgressio illa totum genus humanum morti obnoxium fecit.
latin.433: Tu hoc adscribis justitiae Dei, quae transgressionem illam praecisam ab insecuta corruptione nobis omnibus, hoc ipso quod Adami filii sumus, imputet immediate, non secus ac si eam ipsi, qui tum nulli eramus, admisisseimus, ac consequenter nos primum inflictâ corruptione morali quae peccatum est, & causa omnium nostrorum peccatorum, deinde morte corporis & aeterna, puniat. Itaque vis transgressionem illam actualem nos fecisse morti obnoxios interventu eiusmodi imputationis. Ego vero absque tali imputatione aio transgressionem illam naturali efficientia & sequela vitiasse facultates Adami, etiam illam qua nos genuit, eas vero vitiatas genuisse prolem vitiatam, hanc aliam, & ita vitium propagatum & multiplicatum una cum natura humana ad omnes homines, uno Christo excepto, pervenisse sola lege naturae, qua sui quodque simile gignit, quam generalem legem non ad homines solum, sed ad alias etiam Creaturas, quotquot generandi facultate praeditae sunt, pertinentem, & decreto antecedente de creando mundo & natura constituenda positam & sancitam, non decuit Deum ob Adami transgressionem vel abrogare, vel infringere.
latin.434: Itaque laudo haec verba Thomae Aquinatis. Singulis nobis medullitus inest vere & proprie peccatum, non quidem actuale, sed, ut ita loquar, habituale, dignum non temporali modo morte, sed aeterna etiam, quod nostri adversus Pontificios solent multis argumentis evincere, quae tu proculdubio & legisti, & probas. Nos ergo transgressio Adami fecit obnoxios morti corporali & aeternae interventu inhaerentis vitii & culpae, quo nos infecit. Hoc autem vitium in Adamo naturali sequela produxit; ab Adamo vero in nos haud aliter quam ipsa natura humana propagatum est generatione carnali. Volui statum quaestionis hoc loco repetere, quoniam eum purgatum & enucleatum habere perpetuo ob oculos nos decet, ne ab eo aliquando aberrantes in inanes λογομαχίας prolabamur.
latin.435: Quamvis autem conclusionem huius tui syllogismi admittam, tamen non sunt ita liquida praemissae, quin aliqua distinctione egeant, ad rem quam agimus, utili. Nam quomodo, quaeso, intelligis has propositiones, Dominum legem illam dedisse non tantum Adamo, sed etiam posteris omnibus; lege illa interdictum fuisse hominibus esum illius fructus? Distinguenda certe sunt tempora. Nam si Adamus in paradiso liberos genuissent, eos, postea quam geniti fuissent, interdictum illud obligasset; nisi forte interdictum illud Deus tandem abrogasset; quis enim novit mentem Domini? Positiva lex fuit, libertatem arbitrii Adami circa rem natura sua indifferentem circumscribens, ac proinde potuit ad tempus praescribi, eoque tempore elapso abrogari, quemadmodum leges de ciborum delectu, quas Deus olim tulerat populo suo. Quis nostrum scire potest, utrum Deus voluisset interdictum illud perpetuo vigere, an vero ad certum quoddam tempus duntaxat, quo exacto, & probata abunde hominis obedientia, illud sustulisset, facta homini copia utendi in posterum illa arbore? Haud enim decet nos in Dei arcana irrumpere, aut ea quae ignoramus confidenter asseverare.
latin.436: Concedo tamen libenter futurum fuisse ut obligaret posteros Adami quo tempore fuissent, at quo tempore non fuissent, eos tunc ad id observandum fuisse obligatos nullo modo concedere possum. Ipsa naturae lex a qua nemo eximi potest, non obligat ad obedientiam, nisi eos, qui sunt in rerum natura, & quamdiu sunt in rerum natura. Qui nondum sunt in Mundum ingressi, nondum tenentur observare leges latas iis qui sunt in Mundo. Acceperant Israelitae olim legem in deserto pro se & posteris; quis credat eo tempore, quo peregrinabantur in eodem deserto, Davidem, aut Mariam Virginem debuisse iam tunc legem illam observare? aut propterea eorum qui primi legem acceperunt, peccata fuisse posteris imputanda omnibus ad saeculorum usque consummationem?

pass_a.431: Cap. VIII opens Placeus's reply to arguments drawn from the Old Testament (his opponent's Cap. V) for imputing Adam's actual sin. With the status of the question set out as the learned man pleased, Placeus says that in his fifth chapter he now draws his argument-forces into the field and unfolds them. First in line come a few drawn from the Old Testament.
pass_a.432: The first breaks out from the interdict of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: if that ban and threat looked not only to the first parents but to the whole human race, then the breach of that command made not only them but the whole race liable to death—and the prior is true, so the latter. The major's first part (about the interdict) is outside controversy: who denies the Lord gave the law not only to Adam but to all posterity, or that by that law all were forbidden that fruit? The consequence shows in the event: when the ban was broken, Adam and all posterity became liable to death. Placeus first concedes the conclusion—it fits his view as well as his opponent's: he firmly believes with him that Adam's transgression made the whole race liable to death. The question between them is only the mode.
pass_a.433: The opponent ascribes that mode to God's justice, which immediately imputes that transgression, cut off from the following corruption, to us all just because we are Adam's sons—as if we who then were nothing had committed it—and then punishes us first with inflicted moral corruption (sin and cause of all our sins), then with bodily and eternal death. So he wants that actual transgression to have made us liable to death by such imputation's intervention. Placeus without such imputation says that transgression by natural efficiency and sequel vitiated Adam's faculties—including that by which he begot us—and those vitiated faculties begot vitiated offspring, and so the vice propagated with human nature to all (Christ alone excepted) by nature's law alone whereby like begets like—a general law binding not only humans but other generating creatures, set by the antecedent decree of creating the world—which it did not become God to abrogate or break for Adam's transgression.
pass_a.434: So Placeus praises Thomas Aquinas's words. In each of us there truly and properly is sin deep in the marrow—not actual but, so to speak, habitual—worthy not only of temporal but of eternal death, which our side usually proves against the Papists with many arguments the opponent has doubtless read and approves. Therefore Adam's transgression made us liable to bodily and eternal death by intervening inherent vice and fault with which it infected us. That vice in Adam natural sequel produced; from Adam into us it was propagated no otherwise than human nature itself by carnal generation. Placeus restates the status of the question here so we keep it purged and clarified always before our eyes, lest straying we fall into empty logomachies.
pass_a.435: Though he admits the syllogism's conclusion, the premises are not so clear they need no useful distinction. How does the opponent understand that the Lord gave that law not only to Adam but to all posterity, and that by it eating that fruit was forbidden to men? Times must be distinguished. If Adam had begotten children in paradise, that interdict would have bound them after they were born—unless God at last abrogated it; who knows the Lord's mind? It was positive law fencing Adam's free choice about a thing indifferent by nature, and so could be prescribed for a time and abrogated when that time elapsed, like the food-choice laws God once gave his people. Who of us can know whether God meant that ban to stand forever, or only for a certain time after which, obedience amply proved, he would have lifted it and given man free use of that tree thereafter? It does not become us to break into God's secrets or confidently assert what we do not know.
pass_a.436: Placeus gladly concedes it would have bound Adam's posterity at the time they existed; that they were bound to keep it at the time they did not yet exist he cannot concede at all. Nature's own law, from which none can be exempted, does not bind to obedience except those who are in existence, and while they are. Those not yet entered into the world are not yet held to observe laws made for those in the world. Israel once received the law in the desert for themselves and posterity—who believes that while they wandered there David or the Virgin Mary already owed to keep that law then? Or that therefore the sins of the first receivers must be imputed to all posterity to the consummation of the ages? Tip before the infant / Hypognosticon deepen.

431: CHAPTER VIII. Reply to the arguments which for the Imputation of Adam's Actual sin are drawn from the Old Testament, Cap. V. The status of the question having been constituted and illustrated as it seemed good to you, at length, most distinguished Sir, in the fifth chapter of your treatise you draw the forces of your arguments into the field and unfold them. And first of all there come forth a few drawn from the Old Testament.
432: The first breaks out from the interdict of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and proceeds thus. If that interdict, you say, and the threat looked not only to the first parents but also to the whole human race, it follows that the transgression of that Command made not only the first parents liable to death, but also the whole human race. But the prior is true. Therefore the latter also. The first part of the major (which concerns the interdict) is outside controversy: for who will deny that the Lord gave the law not only to Adam but also to all posterity? Who will deny that by that law eating of that fruit was forbidden to all men? And the consequence is manifest from the event: for when the interdict was violated, both Adam and all posterity were made liable to death. At the outset I concede the conclusion of this argument of yours: for it is friendly to my opinion as well as to yours. I believe firmly with you that Adam's transgression made not only the first parents liable to death, but also the whole human race. But the question between us is only about the mode by which that transgression made the whole human race liable to death.
433: You ascribe this to God's justice, which immediately imputes that transgression, cut off from the corruption that followed, to us all, by this very fact that we are sons of Adam, not otherwise than if we ourselves, who then were nothing, had committed it, and consequently punishes us first with inflicted moral corruption which is sin and the cause of all our sins, then with death of the body and eternal death. So you want that actual transgression to have made us liable to death by the intervention of such imputation. But I say without such imputation that that transgression by natural efficiency and sequel vitiated Adam's faculties, even that by which he begot us, and that those vitiated faculties begot vitiated offspring, and this another, and so the vice, propagated and multiplied together with human nature, reached all men, Christ alone excepted, by the sole law of nature whereby each thing begets its like—which general law, belonging not only to men but also to other Creatures endowed with the faculty of generating, and set and sanctioned by the antecedent decree concerning creating the world and constituting nature, it did not become God to abrogate or infringe because of Adam's transgression.
434: So I praise these words of Thomas Aquinas. In each of us there is truly and properly sin deep in the marrow, not indeed actual, but, so to speak, habitual, worthy not only of temporal death but of eternal also, which our side usually prove against the Papists with many arguments which you have doubtless both read and approve. We, therefore, Adam's transgression made liable to bodily and eternal death by the intervention of the inherent vice and fault with which it infected us. But this vice in Adam natural sequel produced; and from Adam into us it was propagated no otherwise than human nature itself by carnal generation. I wanted to repeat the status of the question in this place, because it becomes us to keep it purged and clarified perpetually before our eyes, lest sometime straying from it we slide into empty logomachies.
435: Although I admit the conclusion of this syllogism of yours, yet the premises are not so clear that they do not need some distinction useful to the matter we are treating. For how, I ask, do you understand these propositions—that the Lord gave that law not only to Adam but also to all posterity; that by that law eating of that fruit was forbidden to men? Times certainly must be distinguished. For if Adam had begotten children in paradise, that interdict would have bound them after they had been born—unless perhaps God at last abrogated that interdict; for who knows the mind of the Lord? It was a positive law, fencing Adam's freedom of choice about a thing indifferent by its own nature, and so could be prescribed for a time and, that time elapsed, abrogated, just as the laws about choice of foods which God once laid down for his people. Who of us can know whether God had willed that interdict to be in force forever, or only for some certain time, which being finished, and man's obedience amply proved, he would have taken away, man being given freedom thereafter to use that tree? For it does not become us to break into God's secrets, or confidently to assert what we do not know.
436: I concede freely, however, that it would have bound Adam's posterity at the time they existed; but that at the time they did not exist they were then bound to observe it I can in no way concede. Nature's own law, from which no one can be exempted, does not bind to obedience except those who are in the nature of things, and as long as they are in the nature of things. Those who have not yet entered into the World are not yet held to observe laws laid down for those who are in the World. The Israelites once received the law in the desert for themselves and their posterity; who would believe that at that time, while they were wandering in the same desert, David, or the Virgin Mary, already then owed to observe that law? Or that therefore the sins of those who first received the law were to be imputed to all posterity even to the consummation of the ages?
